title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) .../... of 9.7.2026 supplementing Regulation (EU) 2024/3012 by establishing the certification methodologies for carbon farming activities (C(2026) 4666 final)
date_evidence:
Council of the
European Union
Brussels, 10 July 2026
(OR. en)
11809/26
key_claim: The delegated act adopted on 9 July 2026 establishes certification methodologies for three carbon farming activities: agriculture and agroforestry on mineral soils, rewetting and restoration of peatlands and other organic soils, and afforestation. Recital 9 states that carbon farming revenues might drive up land prices and lead to land speculation, that EU-wide data on revenues and opportunity costs remain scarce, and that it is currently not possible to quantify indirect land use change emissions or land speculation risks. Recital 13 defers safeguards against land speculation and a common practice test to future knowledge-sharing events. Recital 11 provides that soil emission reduction units from peatland rewetting and improved fertiliser use are irreversible so that no liability mechanism is needed. Recital 8 sets an uncertainty deduction factor of at least 10%. The draft drew 252 feedback submissions between 22 January and 19 February 2026, and the length of activity and monitoring periods was among the provisions changed in response.
frame_summary: The Commission is arguing that the technical and integrity questions on carbon farming certification are now settled enough to proceed, and that the distributional and land-market consequences can be observed and addressed later once the scheme has generated evidence.
verbatim_quote: In addition, the potential revenues generated through carbon farming practices might drive up land prices, leading to land speculation.
verbatim_list: Therefore, currently it is not possible to quantify ILUC emissions or land speculation risks, pending experience with regard to the application of Regulation (EU) 2024/3012 and the availability of information on prices for certified units, income foregone from lost yields, and land values.

In order to reflect experience with the application of this Regulation and with the adoption of carbon farming practices in the Union, also with a view to include a common practice test and safeguards against land speculation, knowledge sharing events should be organised for collecting feedback and sharing best practices,
the soil emission reductions units generated from those activities are therefore irreversible, with the consequence that no liability mechanism is needed

During this period, 252 feedback submissions were received including from 86 companies/businesses, 48 business associations, 44 nongovernmental organisations, 21 EU citizens, 19 public authorities, 6 environmental organisations, 18 academic/research institutions, and one trade union.

As a result, some changes and clarifications have been added to the draft, especially in the length of activity and monitoring periods, the renewal of activity periods, the quantification of peatland emissions, and risk assessment methodologies.
notes: Primary legal instrument, transmitted to the Council on 10 July 2026 as document 11809/26. The recitals are the load-bearing evidence for the scan: the Commission names the land-price and speculation risk, declines to quantify it, and defers the safeguard. Quote provenance: verbatim_quote and verbatim_list confirmed by hand against the live PDF at compose time on 2026-09-22.

title: Commission adopts certification methodologies for carbon farming under the CRCF Regulation
date_evidence:
- News article
- 10 July 2026
- Directorate-General for Climate Action
- 2 min read
key_claim: DG Climate Action announced on 10 July 2026 that the Commission had adopted three certification methodologies for carbon farming under the CRCF Regulation, covering agriculture and agroforestry on mineral soils, peatland and organic-soil rewetting, and afforestation. The Commission presents the methodologies as a route for farmers, foresters and land managers to access financial rewards and a new source of income. Once the Delegated Regulation is in force, certification schemes can apply for recognition against these methodologies and the minimum requirements in Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2358.
frame_summary: The Commission is presenting the adoption as the arrival of a credible income stream for land managers and a milestone in EU climate action, with the emphasis on integrity and farmer reward rather than on who within the land-holding chain captures that reward.
verbatim_quote: By providing a trusted certification framework, the new methodologies can help farmers, foresters, and land managers access financial rewards, creating a new source of income that supports the uptake of sustainable land management practices.
notes: The official framing the scan tests against the delegated act's own recitals. Quote provenance: confirmed by hand against the live page at compose time on 2026-09-22.

title: Agricultural land prices and rents: statistics
date_evidence:
Data extracted in January 2026

Planned article update: January 2027
key_claim: In 2024 the average price of one hectare of arable land in the EU was 15,224 euro, which Eurostat states was 38 times the average annual rental price of 403 euro per hectare of arable land. The average rental price of arable land and permanent grassland combined was 295 euro per hectare. Arable land prices ranged from 4,825 euro per hectare in Latvia to 201,263 euro in Malta, and at regional level from 1,933 euro in Ovre Norrland in Sweden to 187,109 euro in Flevoland in the Netherlands. Data were extracted in January 2026 and the article is updated annually.
frame_summary: Eurostat is presenting land price and rent data as the measure by which policymakers judge whether farms remain viable and whether land prices are driving structural change, treating the capital value of land as the variable policy should watch.
verbatim_quote: In 2024, the average price of one hectare of arable land in the EU was €15 224. This average price was 38 times more than the average annual rental price of €403 per hectare of arable land.
verbatim_list: Within the EU, the average rental price of arable land and / or permanent grassland was €295 per hectare in 2024.
notes: Evergreen Eurostat Statistics Explained article, refreshed annually; data extracted January 2026, accessed 22 September 2026. Supplies the ratio that makes the distributional point: the capital value of a hectare is 38 times its annual rent, so anything that moves land value dwarfs anything that moves annual income. Quote provenance: verbatim_quote confirmed by hand against the live page at compose time on 2026-09-22.

title: Farm tenure
date_evidence:
Data from April 2024

Planned article update: 10 September 2026
key_claim: Rented land accounted for 46% of the total utilised agricultural area in the EU in 2020, against 48% owned and farmed by its manager, with common land at 3% and share farming and other tenure modes at 4%. Rented land was a majority of the utilised agricultural area in 11 EU countries, highest in Bulgaria at 77%, Slovakia at 74%, Malta at 74% and Czechia at 73%. Almost two-thirds of rented farmland, 65.4%, sat on farms of over 100 hectares, against 38.7% of owned farmland. Between 2010 and 2020 rented area rose by an estimated 1.5 million hectares while owner-farmed area fell by an estimated 5.6 million hectares.
frame_summary: Eurostat is arguing that tenure security is an enabler of farm investment and of generational renewal, and treats the split between owned and rented land as a structural feature of EU agriculture rather than an incidental one.
verbatim_quote: Across the EU as a whole, rented land accounted for 46 % of the total utilised agricultural area in 2020, only a very slightly lower share than that for land that was owned and farmed by its manager (48 %).
verbatim_list: This proportion was higher still among rented land and contrasted starkly with owned farmland; almost two-thirds (65.4 %) of rented farmland was on farms of over 100 hectares compared with about two fifths (38.7 %) of owned farmland (see Figure 2).

Although the amount of utilised agricultural area in the EU declined by an estimated 1.1 million hectares between 2010 and 2020 to 157.4 million hectares, the amount of land that was rented increased by an estimated 1.5 million hectares, whilst the amount of own-land farmed declined by an estimated 5.6 million hectares.
notes: Evergreen Eurostat Statistics Explained article carrying 2020 Farm Structure Survey data, accessed 22 September 2026. The 46% figure is the structural fact the signal turns on. Note the source writes percentages as '46 %'; the scan renders them in house style as 46%. Quote provenance: verbatim_quote confirmed by hand against the live page at compose time on 2026-09-22.

title: Policy layering in EU carbon farming governance: insights from eight EU Member States, Environmental Sciences Europe 38(147)
key_claim: A peer-reviewed study of expert perceptions across eight EU Member States finds that carbon-farming practices are currently supported mainly through existing CAP instruments rather than coherent stand-alone carbon farming strategies, and interprets the CRCF as policy layering: a new governance instrument added on top of established agricultural and climate policy without changing the existing structure. The authors identify the absence of reliable demand structures for CRCF credits and incompatibilities between CRCF certification and national climate accounting as pointing towards an inefficient and counter-productive outcome, and warn the CRCF risks remaining a layered instrument with low climate impact.
frame_summary: The authors are arguing that the CRCF has been added on top of existing agricultural policy rather than integrated into it, and that without demand and accounting integration the certification will change paperwork and incentive rhetoric more than it changes land management.
verbatim_quote: Unless these challenges are addressed, the CRCF risks remaining a layered instrument without real integration into national policy frameworks and with low climate impact.
verbatim_list: the absence of reliable demand structures for CRCF credits and structural incompatibilities between CRCF certification and national climate accounting systems point towards an inefficient outcome and counter-productive layering, respectively
notes: Peer-reviewed open-access research article, Environmental Sciences Europe volume 38, article number 147 (2026), Springer. Used for the demand-side and integration limb of the argument and as part of the counter-case. Publisher field records Springer to match the host domain; the article is published in the Springer open-access journal Environmental Sciences Europe, which is the label used on the inline citation. Quote provenance: verbatim_quote confirmed by hand against the live page at compose time on 2026-09-22.

title: What can we take away from the Commission's first CRCF Days?
key_claim: Reporting from the Commission's first CRCF Days on 20-21 May 2026, Carbon Gap records that the European carbon farming pipeline could reach 420 million tonnes of CO2 by 2040, with 20 million tonnes immediately available when CRCF methodologies launch, two-thirds of it removals and one-third emission reductions, against a global market valued at 300 million dollars in 2024. It records that high unit economics, price volatility, a weakening regulatory environment in 2025 and the absence of long-term offtake agreements are constraining bankability, and that the carbon farming track of the EU Carbon Removal Buyers' Club, designed with Deloitte, targets operational launch in early 2027, with a complementary EU facility from 2027.
frame_summary: Carbon Gap is arguing that Europe has built the supply-side integrity architecture for carbon removal ahead of the demand architecture, and that the binding task now is to coordinate buyers into contracted offtake before the pipeline stalls.
verbatim_quote: High unit economics, price volatility, a weakening regulatory environment in 2025, and the absence of long-term offtake agreements are all constraining bankability.
verbatim_list: Carbon farming opportunity is real and large. The European pipeline could reach 420M tonnes CO₂ by 2040, with 20M tonnes immediately available when CRCF methodologies launch.
notes: Structural anchor. At 123 days it sits in the 3-6 month band, but it is the canonical account of the demand-side state of play at the point the methodologies were finalised, and no in-window equivalent exists. Carbon Gap is a registered charity and policy research organisation; classified Tier 2 as an institutional research body, with the caveat that it advocates for carbon removal scale-up. Quote provenance: verbatim_quote confirmed by hand against the live page at compose time on 2026-09-22.

title: New AlliedOffsets Report Looks Into Soil Carbon's 2026 Momentum
key_claim: Reporting AlliedOffsets market data, Carbon Herald states that the buyer base for soil carbon credits has grown from 80 buyers in 2022 to 128 in 2026, with Microsoft, Shell, NW Natural and PetroChina among the top offtakers and retirers. Soil carbon supply is not broad-based: Northern Rangelands Trust is the single largest issuer by a wide margin, and supply is geographically concentrated, with India dominating forecast future issuance ahead of Kenya, China and Brazil. Forecast issuance is projected to peak in the early 2040s before declining as the crediting periods of currently active projects end.
frame_summary: Carbon Herald and AlliedOffsets are arguing that 2026 is soil carbon's most newsworthy year but that the market remains narrow on both sides, with concentrated supply and a buyer base still counted in the low hundreds.
verbatim_quote: The buyer base for soil carbon credits has grown from 80 buyers in 2022 to 128 in 2026, with the list of top offtakes and retirees including brands such as Microsoft, Shell, NW Natural, and PetroChina.
verbatim_list: Forecasted issuance is projected to peak in the early 2040s before declining, based on a model of currently active projects and their crediting periods coming to an end.
notes: Specialist trade press reporting a commercial data provider's market report; used only as directional corroboration on the thinness of the buyer base. Quote provenance: confirmed by hand against the live page at compose time on 2026-09-22.
